name: Price Placebo Effect
description: Price and other marketing cues can change the experience itself, not just what people say about it afterward. A 'premium' frame can make the same product feel more effective, pleasant, or valuable.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in pricing pages, premium-tier framing, packaging, checkout, onboarding promises, and any interface cue that sets expectations before use.
myth_risk_note: Only four directly on-topic papers were found in this pass, and none explicitly test failed replications -- rated moderate on the basis of this pass's thin yield, not a reversal of the concept's existing backing.
prevalence_note: Common in pricing, branding, CRO, and premium-experience design discussions; less central than defaults or social proof in general UX curricula, but a well-known lever in behavioral marketing practice.

findings.description: An inert pill framed as a discounted-price pain medication produced less self-reported pain relief from electric-shock stimuli than the identical inert pill framed as full-price, showing the price-driven placebo/expectancy effect generalizes from a consumer-performance context to an actual clinical/analgesic outcome measure.
findings.source_title: Commercial Features of Placebo and Therapeutic Efficacy

findings.description: Consumers who paid a discounted price for an identical energy drink marketed as boosting mental acuity solved fewer puzzles afterward than consumers who paid the regular price for the same drink — a genuine downstream performance difference, not just a reported-satisfaction difference — mediated by price-driven efficacy expectancies operating largely outside conscious awareness.
findings.source_title: Placebo Effects of Marketing Actions: Consumers May Get What They Pay For

findings.description: Raising the price label on an objectively identical wine sample increased both participants' subjective flavor-pleasantness ratings and BOLD activity in medial orbitofrontal cortex — a region associated with encoding experienced pleasantness — indicating that price-driven expectancy effects on perceived quality are reflected in measurable neural activity, not merely in self-report bias.
findings.source_title: Marketing actions can modulate neural representations of experienced pleasantness
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

applications.title: The Coke/Pepsi brand-label effect: a decades-old marketing challenge later confirmed in the brain itself
applications.description: PepsiCo's ongoing 'Pepsi Challenge' marketing campaign, running blind taste tests in public since 1975, produced a well-known and durable puzzle: consumers frequently preferred Pepsi's taste in blind tests, yet Coca-Cola continued to dominate branded sales by a wide margin. In 2004, McClure, Li, Tomlin, Cypert, Montague & Montague (Neuron, Vol. 44, No. 2, pp. 379-387) investigated the same effect directly, giving 67 volunteers Coke and Pepsi both blind and with the brand known, while scanning their brains via fMRI. Knowing the brand changed subjects' reported preference and activated brain regions associated with emotion, memory, and cultural identity (the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and hippocampus) differently than the blind condition -- brand information measurably altered the subjective experience of an identical product, not merely what people said about it afterward.
applications.industry_context: Consumer packaged goods / beverage marketing, later cited as a founding case in the emerging field of neuromarketing.
applications.ethical_note: Coca-Cola's decades of brand investment plausibly deliberately cultivate exactly this psychological effect, which is a real persuasion dimension worth naming -- but the underlying product itself isn't misrepresented (the consumer's own genuine subjective experience is what changes, not a false claim about what's in the can), and the neuroscience paper itself frames this as a finding about culture and memory rather than an accusation of manipulation. Graded unclear rather than forcing a verdict the source doesn't itself support.
